extracted.intended_audience: voters/ratifiers of the proposed U.S. Constitution; citizens of New York; constitutional designers
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive principles and practical criteria for structuring national defense authority in a constitution: who may raise and maintain forces, how funding should be constrained, and why restraints on legislative discretion are dangerous or impractical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centralization of military authority under the national government
rubrics_metrics.description: The national forces should be in the hands of the national government rather than the separate States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate possession of military forces by States would be inequitable and unsafe (some states more exposed than others), create mutual jealousy, encourage counterpoises, and produce military establishments 'apt to swell beyond their natural or proper size' that could be used to abridge or demolish national authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid leaving defense burdens to individual States
rubrics_metrics.description: It would be neither equitable nor safe for a single State (e.g., New York) to bear the whole weight of establishments requisite to its immediate safety and that of its neighbors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If defense burdens fall unevenly, the security of all depends on the 'parsimony, improvidence, or inability' of a part; concentration of force in a few states would alarm others and spur dangerous countermeasures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not fetter legislative discretion with impracticable restraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Constitutional restrictions that cannot be observed in practice (e.g., absolute prohibitions on military establishments) are improper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such restrictions will be disregarded when necessity arises, and frequent breaches of fundamental laws erode reverence for the constitution and create precedents for further breaches; lawmakers should avoid 'fetters' that cannot be consistently followed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ambiguous prohibitions (use clear, practicable language)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provisions that say armies 'ought not' be kept up rather than 'shall not' are ambiguous and reflect conflict between jealousy and conviction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ambiguous language invites interpretation as mere admonition and will cease to operate when legislators incline to disregard it (as illustrated by state constitutions that say armies 'ought not' be kept up).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on keeping armies in peacetime is impractical
rubrics_metrics.description: A constitutional ban on keeping or even raising armies in time of peace would incapacitate a nation from preparing for defence before invasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because formal declarations of war are less common, waiting until invasion to raise forces would leave the nation unable to 'anticipate distant danger' and invite attack; therefore, absolute bans on raising or keeping armies in peacetime are unsafe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit appropriations for the army to short, renewable periods (two-year check)
rubrics_metrics.description: Restrain the permanence of military funding by limiting appropriations for the support of an army to the period of two years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This forces the legislature to deliberate periodically, provides opportunities for public scrutiny and opposition parties to sound alarms, involves State legislatures as jealous guardians, and makes long conspiracies to subvert liberty through gradual army growth less feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Periodic legislative review as an effective democratic check
rubrics_metrics.description: Requiring periodic (biennial) reauthorization of army support keeps the issue before the people and alerts opponents to object and organize.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Biennial appropriations ensure the legislature cannot vest permanent military funds in the executive; party opposition and state legislatures will have chances to 'sound the alarm' and mobilize public opinion if majority inclinations threaten liberties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Militia alone is an unreliable bulwark
rubrics_metrics.description: The country cannot rely solely on militia for national defense; regular, disciplined forces are sometimes necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experience (the Revolutionary War) showed militia—despite bravery—could not by themselves establish or secure liberty against regular, disciplined armies; war is a 'science' requiring training, perseverance, and practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimate need for standing forces in certain emergencies
rubrics_metrics.description: There will be situations (large insurrections, invasions, or widespread disorder) where the militia is inadequate and a different kind of force must be employed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States themselves have raised regular troops to quell insurrections; hence, it is unreasonable to object to a national government having the option to do likewise in extraordinary emergencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger of executive-legislative collusion must be considered but mitigated, not eliminated
rubrics_metrics.description: While combinations between executive and legislature could fabricate pretenses to maintain forces, such dangers do not justify impracticable prohibitions; instead, use institutional checks like periodic appropriations and public vigilance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that the executive could retain a force large enough to dispense with legislative supplies are countered by asking how such a force could be created in peacetime without public notice and by pointing to the improbability of perpetual conspiracies surviving elections and public scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on legalistic paradoxes; design powers that meet exigencies
rubrics_metrics.description: A government should possess authority commensurate with possible contingencies; leaving no body able to act in national exigencies is unsafe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: English Bill of Rights prohibited armies without Parliament consent but did not restrict legislative discretion; prudent constitutional design grants a power sufficient for all contingencies and submits its exercise to legislative judgment rather than judicially precise prohibitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal laws should be supreme and state officers integrated into enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Enumerated, legitimate federal laws become the supreme law, and all officers—legislative, executive, judicial—of each State are bound by oath to observe them and can be auxiliary to their enforcement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extending federal authority to individuals enables the national government to use ordinary state magistracy in executing laws, familiarizes citizens with the Union's authority, and reduces the need for force by integrating administration across levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Familiarity and regular federal presence reduces need for coercion
rubrics_metrics.description: The more the national authority operates in ordinary life, the more it will be respected and supported, diminishing the occasions where force would be required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When federal government actions are intermingled with daily political life and citizens meet it frequently, affection and obedience increase; a government 'continually at a distance' will have less influence and may require more force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid constitutional provisions that are redundant or meaningless
rubrics_metrics.description: Declaring that acts should not be done without consent of the legislature is redundant when that legislature already exclusively holds the power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such redundant clauses (e.g., state constitutions saying armies 'ought not' be kept up 'without the consent of the legislature') add nothing and can create confusion about who legitimately holds authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precise draftsmanship: 'ought not' vs 'shall not' affects enforceability
rubrics_metrics.description: Choice of words (admonition v. prohibition) materially affects whether a provision will operate as a binding restriction or a mere recommendation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States that used 'ought not' instead of 'shall not' effectively created cautionary statements that could be ignored when inconvenient; constitutional drafters should prefer language that reflects the intended practical effect.
